title: Signal Daily — AI — 2026-10-02
summary: Three stories. Epoch AI estimates that the cost of a fixed level of AI performance has fallen about 47% per quarter. arXiv announced a change to submission rate limits. An essay by Yedhu Krishnan and an accompanying developer discussion examine why engineers should write commit descriptions themselves as a thinking tool rather than delegating them to AI.

stories.headline: The cost of a given AI performance level has fallen about 47% per quarter
stories.dek: Epoch AI estimates a 13x annual drop in the price of hitting a fixed benchmark score, a pace it says outruns measured declines for DNA sequencing, compute, and lithium-ion batteries.
tldr: Epoch AI estimates that the cost of a given level of AI performance has fallen about 47% per quarter, or 13x per year, over the past three years.
On GPQA Diamond, the report estimates that o3 reached a 75% score at $0.30 per question on January 31, 2025, while GPT-5.6 Luna later matched that score at $0.0004.
Epoch says the decline slows after a performance level debuts, from 66% per quarter to 32% per quarter two years later, and flags benchmaxxing plus incomplete data as caveats.

body.text: Epoch AI's September 22, 2026 report, "The plunging price of thought," estimates that the cost of reaching a given level of AI performance has fallen about 47% per quarter, or 13x per year, across five benchmarks covering mathematics, hard sciences, and games of skill. In log points, the authors say that pace is four times faster than DNA sequencing, six times faster than compute, and 18 times faster than lithium-ion batteries.

The report's GPQA Diamond example estimates that OpenAI's o3, released January 31, 2025, could reach a 75% score at an average of $0.30 per question. Just under 18 months later, GPT-5.6 Luna matched that score at $0.0004 per question, a 725-fold drop. Epoch notes that its "75%" figure is 75% of the way from chance to a perfect score, which is 81.25% on this four-way exam.

Epoch says the drop is not one curve. Game-based puzzles fell about 39–43% per quarter, while math problems fell 50–52% per quarter. Across the five benchmarks, cost falls 66% per quarter when a performance level is new and 32% per quarter two years later. The authors warn that benchmark-specific training, which they call benchmaxxing, can make measured gains look steeper than real-world work, and that buyers who do not switch to the cheapest capable model will not capture the full saving.

TechSpot's October 1 report on the Epoch findings says cheaper access to a given capability could make more capable models affordable for everyday software use and make it harder for AI developers to hold onto pricing power. It also notes that the historical comparisons use uneven windows: the AI series is recent, the compute series ends in 2001, and the electricity series ends in 1973.

stories.whyItMatters: A falling price for a fixed benchmark score changes what software buyers can afford, but Epoch's own caveat is that the figure is the cheapest model on a test, not the cost of a finished job. If labs keep raising the capability bar while inference prices fall, spending on chips, power, and frontier training can stay high even as a single question gets cheaper. That split sits on both the AI supply chain and the software market that buys the output.
stories.editorNote: Operator's view, recorded here as the editor's note: two forces are speeding the drop in AI cost — hardware improvement becoming general, and efficiency. Frontier labs such as OpenAI and Anthropic still face rising build costs, knowledge that once circulated as a public good is being absorbed into proprietary systems and sold, and the practical counterweight is models efficient enough to run on local machines. This view is not an Epoch finding. The report prices the cheapest route to a benchmark score. It does not establish hardware as the main cause, and it already costs some open-weight models on rented hardware. Smaller local models are already in use. stories.headline: ArXiv's Updated Rate Limit Policy
stories.dek: arXiv announced a new submission rate-limit policy, framing it as a temporary response to rising submissions and moderation capacity.
tldr: arXiv announced an updated rate-limit policy for submissions.
The repository described the change as a stopgap while it reviews practices around AI-assisted submissions and improves moderation tools.
Terence Tao separately discussed the policy, while the collected material does not establish its longer-term effects.

body.text: arXiv's October 1 announcement says the updated submission limits apply across submitters and categories as a temporary measure while the repository reviews practices for AI-assisted work and improves its moderation processes.

Terence Tao also covered the policy on his blog. The available sources establish the announcement and its stated rationale, but do not yet show how the limit will affect submission patterns or moderation outcomes.

stories.whyItMatters: The policy directly changes the operating rules of a major preprint repository as AI tools lower the practical barriers to producing manuscripts. Its stated temporary status leaves the eventual moderation approach open.

stories.headline: Why Developers Still Write Commit Descriptions by Hand in the AI Era
stories.dek: Yedhu Krishnan argues that drafting commit messages remains an essential thinking tool to verify human understanding and prevent AI-fabricated rationale.
tldr: Yedhu Krishnan writes that AI agents lack offline context and invent plausible reasons when drafting commit descriptions, risking distorted project history.
Writing commit rationales by hand forces human developers to reflect on AI-generated changes, test understanding, and record unstated exit criteria.
A Hacker News discussion on the post highlights that human-written commit descriptions are critical to explain 'why' and prevent runaway technical debt.

body.text: Yedhu Krishnan wrote on September 30, 2026, that developers in the agentic coding era face new risks when relying on AI to write commit descriptions. When an AI agent lacks offline and cross-tool context, Krishnan observes that it invents its own plausible rationale for changes, creating fabricated histories that diverge from real decisions.

Even when given complete context, Krishnan argues that allowing an AI to draft the explanation misses the primary value of a commit message: verifying that the human developer understands what is being shipped. He writes that explaining the "why" in one's own words serves as a thinking tool and cognitive check to ensure the code matches intent and captures unwritten exit criteria.

A Hacker News discussion on the essay drew over 70 comments, where software engineers underscored that delegating entire implementations and commit drafting to AI agents risks accumulating fragile technical debt. Multiple practitioners noted that diffs explain what changed, while human-written rationales remain essential to document constraints, rejected alternatives, and operational assumptions.

stories.whyItMatters: As AI agents generate an increasing share of production code, the bottleneck shifts from writing implementation syntax to understanding and maintaining system behavior. Treating commit descriptions as an active human thinking step creates an explicit checkpoint against shipping unverified code and establishes whether engineers can still explain the software they operate.
stories.editorNote: Operator's view, recorded here as the editor's note: Coding with AI has improved routine documentation, but documents represent current state updates rather than incremental history. Because code evolves through dozens or hundreds of iterations and accumulates its own history, capturing every step in documents is impractical, especially since documents must reflect current reality so AI can accurately diagnose problems. The operator argues that commit messages should serve as rich, intent-driven logs that record why decisions were made, forming a chronological ledger of code evolution. Future AI systems can then combine current snapshot documentation with historical git commit logs to reconstruct intent and trace architecture, which is vital for understanding code the human did not write. This operator view is not a conclusion of Yedhu Krishnan's post or the Hacker News discussion. Krishnan treats commit writing as a human cognitive check rather than a context pipeline for future AI, and the HN thread emphasizes architectural discipline over snapshot-versus-log documentation.
